en: The *Vyākhyāna* (Exegesis) on the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra*, a commentary composed by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu,
translated by the Indian Tripiṭaka Master Vimokṣasena of Central India during the Northern Wei dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Bhagavān was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great community of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Prajñāsamudravipula-pratibhāna-saṃdarśana, saying:
"Prajñāsamudravipula-pratibhāna-saṃdarśana!
There are two kinds of sustaining power by which a Tathāgata turns the wheel of Dharma."
What are these two? First is the sustenance of sentient beings;
second is the sustenance of the Dharma.
O Wisdom-Encircled Ocean of Eloquence!
These two modes of sustaining the Dharma have been taught by the Tathāgata throughout the turning of the wheel of Dharma, even unto the conclusion of this sūtra.
For what reason is this supreme sūtra of the true wheel of Dharma so called?

That King of Munis is inconceivable, incomparable, ineffable, immeasurable, and beyond analogy, like space; he is neither annihilated nor eternal, entering in accordance with dependent origination. He is the excellence of tranquility, the supreme tranquility, the foremost tranquility, and the ultimate tranquility—truthful, non-false, and real. Thus the Tathāgata turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and proclaims this sūtra.
It is praised by the śrāvakas who are disciples of the Tathāgata, by the disciples of the śrāvakas, and by the various ṛṣis.
For this reason, I shall now provide an explanation.
How is this explained?
For what reason has the Great Muni King, possessed of immeasurable merit, turned this inconceivable, immeasurable, supreme, tranquil, virtuous, and stainless wheel?
1. For what reason is it called the "Exalted Sūtra"?
2. For what reason is he named "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān)?

Originally, the third [question] was missing; 4. For what reason does the Tathāgata reside at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha, maintaining these two kinds of sustenance and turning this wheel of Dharma there rather than in any other place?
5. For what reason is he called the Tathāgata?
6. For what reason is it called the Dharma-wheel?
7. Furthermore, World-Honored One, how many times and in how many ways does he turn the wheel of the Dharma?
8. Furthermore, World-Honored One, you have spoken here of "turning. Why, then, does the Tathāgata’s Dharma-gate of non-arising state that all dharmas neither turn nor revert?
One should understand them thus: they are ultimately unarisen.
If this is the case, how can one avoid that sūtra? That sūtra need not be avoided.
Ninth: Furthermore, if it is said that sentient beings maintain the Dharma, what is meant by "maintaining"?

In the Prajñāpāramitā, the Tathāgata addressed Subhūti, saying: "If the Tathāgata were to speak of 'sentient beings, sentient beings' for the duration of an eon, would there be any sentient beings who undergo birth and extinction?"
Subhūti said: "No, World-Honored One."
"All sentient beings have been pure since beginningless time.
Furthermore, in the *Vimalanāman-sūtra*, the Tathāgata said: "If one dwells in the notion of dharmas, this is a great illness."
If all phenomena of sentient beings are ungraspable, then in what does the World-Honored One abide and maintain himself to turn the wheel of Dharma?
This must be explained.

Tenth, for what reason did the World-Honored One abandon that vast and expansive place adorned with various kinds of excellent and wondrous flowering trees, where immeasurable superior persons and great multitudes gather, and instead turn the wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī—a place with few people—in the Deer Park beneath the shade of the Pāṭalī tree?
These causal conditions must also be explained:
(11) Furthermore, at which location did the Blessed One first sit and turn the wheel of Dharma?
(12) Furthermore, when the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma, how many sentient beings abandoned evil and practiced virtue?
Thirteen: To state it briefly, how does one manifest the sustaining of sentient beings and the sustaining of the Dharma?
Fourteen: All of these are difficult points; they shall be explained below.
That Dharma is now being taught.

For what reason has the World-Honored One—the Perfectly Awakened One who is foremost, stainless, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, indestructible, profoundly deep, and immovable—already taught this sutra, and why does he now further teach this supreme, stainless, vast, and beyond-praise?
The World-Honored One is praised by the sentient beings of the three realms; for what reason, then, do you preach this unsurpassable sūtra that is immeasurable and free from all faults?
This meaning shall now be explained.

The World-Honored One feared that among those in the assembly—gods, asuras, humans, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others—hearing the turning of the wheel of Dharma might give rise to doubt and confusion, not knowing by how many modes of sustaining power the World-Honored One turns the wheel of Dharma.

The World-Honored One, observing the doubting minds of sentient beings, in order to sever those doubts, has therefore preached the turning of the wheel of Dharma through two kinds of sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
The people and devas of the world, With minds full of doubt, gaze upon the Lord of Dharma;
To sever the meaning of their doubts, He has preached this sutra.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One possesses the power of great compassion and has taught this sutra for the benefit of sentient beings.
How does the World-Honored One teach this meaning through the power of great compassion?

Now it is said that the World-Honored One, regarding all sentient beings, knows there are no sentient beings; he knows that all phenomena are like a city of the Gandharvas. Having known this, he turns the wheel of Dharma based upon the sustenance of sentient beings and the sustenance of phenomena.
What is the meaning of this?
The verse says:
Knowing that the world is selfless, Like a phantom or a gandharva city;
The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, has taught the abiding nature of the dharmas of sentient beings.
By manifesting his own power, he is thus able to expound this meaning.

In the world, there is no one else capable of sustaining [the Dharma]; only the Buddha can perform these two kinds of sustenance. Furthermore, there is no one who can turn the wheel of the Dharma as I have turned it.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as the verse says:
"It is not a celestial palace, Nor the abode of an asura, Nor a human realm or a dragon palace; There exists such a sentient being."
First is the Ineffable One, who has transcended faults and extinguished the three types of suffering;
revered and saluted by devas and humans, he excellently turns the supreme wheel.
Furthermore, because one must first endure immeasurable suffering and fulfill immeasurable provisions, one subsequently attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

If a bodhisattva who has only recently begun their practice should hear this and feel fear or weakness in their heart, the Tathāgata, wishing to remove that fear and weakness, reveals this meaning: that through stainless and pure awakening, even if there be immeasurable suffering and immeasurable requirements, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
To demonstrate this wheel of Dharma through immeasurable merit,
the verse says:
"Gold, pearls, and the like, Wives, children, kingdoms, and cities— these he gives as gifts."
Giving away one's head, eyes, marrow, and bones, as well as hands, feet, and so forth—such supreme generosity;
enduring various hardships while upholding the precepts; and the rare attainment of the Buddha-body, whose merit is beyond measure:
these are shown for the sake of those who are doubtful or timid.
The Buddha, with a superior intention, observes the minds of sentient beings and turns the wheel of Dharma through immeasurable merit.

Furthermore, for those who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta—namely those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles—who desire to enter nirvāṇa and dwell in the abandonment of the Mahāyāna, he manifests this meaning to instruct them.
Furthermore, O Supreme Mind, if those of the vehicles of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and so forth enter the abode of nirvāṇa, they will no longer turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
As the verse says:
"With small minds and devoid of compassion, etc., They desire to enter the two types of nirvāṇa."
The Muni preached this sūtra to cause beings to abide in the Supreme Vehicle (agrayāna).
Furthermore, this demonstrates the meaning of how these meritorious persons are gladdened and benefited.
Among all those in the world, there is no teacher of the Wheel of Dharma who is more supreme and peerless than my Teacher.
The verse says:
"If one has already taken refuge in the Buddha, and now takes refuge or shall take refuge again—
the Muni rejoices in such a person and speaks this Sūtra."
This teaching demonstrates that if others who rely on non-Buddhist paths were to lead you toward benefit, it would be so;

however, your teacher does not possess a sublime body adorned with stainless merit through which he turns the wheel of Dharma. Your teacher is no match for this, and he cannot cause you to attain the untainted wholesome dharmas.
The verse says:
Seeing that people in the world rely upon evil associates, the Tathāgata,
for the sake of leading them [to the truth], has preached this jewel of a sutra.
The pacification of the pride of omniscience brings great benefit; this meaning is now demonstrated.
I, as one who possesses all-knowledge, have now newly turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma; how can you claim to be a person of all-knowledge?
The verse says:
The Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma, Which can eliminate the inversions of annihilationism and eternalism;
If one cannot turn the pure wheel, That person is not omniscient.
Seeking the benefit of the vast, supreme fruit and the unsurpassed field of merit, [the Buddha] manifests that he is able to bestow inconceivable rewards.
If there are those who can turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, those who give to them will obtain a great reward.
The verse says:
If there is one who can turn the unsurpassed wheel of the true Dharma,
and one bestows even a small gift upon such a person, they shall obtain incomparable karmic retribution.
Furthermore, to demonstrate the meaning of how the Bodhisattva’s practice results in abundant benefit, the World-Honored One said: "This wheel of Dharma of mine is able to bring great benefit.
Having already performed immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of ascetic practices, I have been able to renounce that which is difficult to renounce."
It is like bailing out the ocean with one's heart without ceasing.
Furthermore, it says: "In my past lives as a māṇava, I gave away both my body and my wife and children."
Furthermore, he said: "In a former birth, when I was King Brahmādatta, I gave away my two beloved sons as a gift, and no regret arose in my mind.
He also said: "In a former birth, when I was King Śūradatta, I gave the most beautiful woman among those of exquisite form, named Sundarī, as a gift to a Brahmin."
Furthermore, he said: "In a previous birth, when I was King Guṇasāgara, I attained dhāraṇīs, and for seven thousand years I did not lie down on my side even once.
He also said: "In a previous birth, when I was the crown prince of King Acintyaguṇaratnaśrī, while still a youth, I had mastered all treatises and expounded them for the sake of sentient beings."

Furthermore, it is said: "In a previous birth, he became the Rishi Kāyabandhu; when his hands and feet were severed from his body, he felt no anger or resentment, and for their sake, he preached the Dharma of patience.
It is also said: "In a previous birth, he became King Candraprabha; when he gave away his head as an act of charity, he felt no anger or resentment."

Furthermore, he said: "In a former life, I was the youth King Whom All Beings Delight to Behold; for twelve years I burned my body with incense as an offering to the Buddha and the Dharma, yet no regret arose in my mind."
Furthermore, he said: "In the past, I manifested as the King who Heals Illness and have already healed all the sufferings of disease among the people of Jambudvīpa.
In this way, I have already performed these various and immeasurable acts of alleviating suffering and distress, bringing great benefit; I have now realized this."
In this way, the Bodhisattva manifests the attainment of fruits through various ascetic practices, thereby manifesting benefit.
The World-Honored One has already spoken this sūtra,
as expressed in these verses:
If such is the primary cause, then through ascetic practices and the extensive renunciation of the body,
one should give whatever is appropriate to those who are poor and beg for alms.
Free from all faults, this is the foremost wheel of tranquility.
It is said that non-defamation is foremost; therefore, I now turn [the wheel].
For what reason is he called the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*)? Because he is worthy of receiving offerings, he is called the World-Honored One.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as demonstrated in the *Bodhicittopadeśa*. One might ask:

for what reason does the Tathāgata reside at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha, sustaining himself in two ways and turning the wheel of Dharma there rather than in any other place? Such an objection would be inconsistent with the truth.
Wherever this [objection] may be raised, it is endless; even if the Blessed One were to travel elsewhere, this same objection would arise, and thus it would be infinite.
There is further meaning, which is demonstrated in the *Bodhicittopadeśa*.
In what sense is one called a Tathāgata?
That meaning shall now be explained:
because he has come according to reality, he is called a Tathāgata.
What dharma is called "suchness" (tathatā)?
Nirvāṇa is called suchness.
Sentient beings and dharmas—those two are not suchness.
As the Blessed One said: "O bhikṣus!
That which is the foremost noble truth, the non-false dharma, is called nirvāṇa.
Because one knows this, it is called "coming" (āgata).
The realm of phonology and the realm of scriptology: as worldly people say, "this person has been born.
What does this clarify?
It clarifies the perfection of wisdom.
The meaning of "coming" (*āgata*) is as follows.
*Nirvāṇa* is called "suchness" (*tathatā*), and knowing and understanding it is called "coming. Because he has perfectly awakened to *nirvāṇa*, he is called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are called "suchness"; because he acts in accordance with all these, he is called the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, these Four Noble Truths are called "Suchness" (*tathatā*); because he has seen them and not others, and because he has come from all those conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), he is called the Tathāgata.
Moreover, all such Buddha-dharmas are called "Suchness"; because he has come from them, this person is called the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, as for the names of the six pāramitās—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom—he has come to perfectly awaken to them; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.

Truly relinquishing [all attachments], one dwells in tranquil wisdom within this suchness (*tathatā*); because one has come from that supreme, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one is called a Tathāgata.

All such bodhisattva stages—namely, the ten stages of Joy, Purity, Radiance, Blazing, Difficult to Conquer, Presence, Far-Going, Immovable, Excellent Intelligence, and Cloud of Dharma—are called "suchness."
He is called the Tathāgata because he has come from that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
he is called the Tathāgata because he has come by way of the Eightfold Path;
and he is called the Tathāgata because he has come with the feet of prajñāpāramitā and the feet of skillful means.
Alternatively, he is called "Thus-Gone" (*tathāgata*). Regarding the term "Thus-Gone": it is called "Thus-Gone" because he teaches according to reality;
furthermore, he is called "Thus-Gone" because once gone, he does not return.
Regarding the meaning by which it is called the "Dharma-wheel," that meaning shall now be explained.
The essence of the Dharma is itself the wheel; therefore, it is called the Dharma-wheel.
For example, in the world, because the substance of copper is a jar, it is called a "copper jar."
Just as a wooden body constitutes a wheel, it is therefore called a "wooden wheel," so too is it here:
the Dharma-body constitutes a wheel, and is therefore called the "Dharma-wheel"; thus it is demonstrated.
What is this Dharma?
It refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*).
This Dharma is a wheel; therefore, it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Furthermore, the meaning of awakening to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is the meaning of the Wheel of Dharma.
Moreover, the meaning of the supreme adornment of all phenomena, as well as the meaning of adoption and abandonment—such meanings as these are called the Wheel of Dharma.
What things are relinquished?
They are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
What things are grasped?
It is said that it takes one to nirvāṇa and can also destroy all afflictions; therefore, it is called a wheel (*cakra*), like the wheel of time,
or like the wheel of the Dharma-king’s governance, which is like the wheel of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
The wheel of light that illuminates all worlds is like the wheel of the constellations.
Furthermore, it is said to be the wheel of the Dharma, the wheel of uninterrupted permanence, and the wheel of non-fixation on the two extremes.
It is also the wheel of non-arising, arising in accordance with causes and conditions.
Furthermore, regarding non-duality: one should know that from the eye and form up to the mind and mental objects, there is no duality.
Regarding the wheel of non-apprehension: this is because the phenomena of the three periods of time cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, it is the wheel of emptiness because it is free from all views;
it is the wheel of signlessness because it contemplates all signs as being devoid of signs;
and it is the wheel of wishlessness because it is free from the three realms.
The wheel of all conceptualization is non-differentiated, because all phenomena are not conceptually differentiated.
Furthermore, in the *Anavatapta-nāgarāja-sūtra*, the Blessed One addressed the nāga king, saying: "O Nāga King Bhadramukha!"
Furthermore, the Wheel of Dharma is truly a practice that is indestructible; it is called a "wheel" because it is equal throughout the three periods of time.
It is a wheel without intrinsic nature, for it is free from the two views of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, it is detached from the wheel because the body is free from defilement;
it does not cling to the wheel because it is free from mind, thought, and consciousness;
it is a wheel without location because it has relinquished all conditioned existence and arising.
Furthermore, it is the wheel of reality (*bhūtacakra*) because it possesses the great vision of reality (*bhūtadarśana*).
Furthermore, it is the wheel of truth (*satyacakra*) because its correct cultivation (*samyak-bhāvanā*) is indestructible.
Furthermore, it is the inexhaustible wheel (*akṣayacakra*) because it demonstrates that which is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, there is the wheel of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), because all phenomena are entirely active within it.
Furthermore, there is the wheel of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), because the prior and posterior limits are not themselves limits.
Furthermore, there is the wheel of suchness (*tathatā*), because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is the absence of intrinsic nature.
It is the wheel of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because all doubts have been observed through meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, it is the wheel of constancy (*nitya*), because the nature of the noble ones (*āryatva*) has been gathered.
Furthermore, it is the wheel of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because no internal or external phenomena are perceived.
Furthermore, it is the wheel of signlessness (*animitta-cakra*), because all signs are not discriminated.
Furthermore, it is the wheel of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-cakra*), because all phenomena (*dharma*) are not grasped as objects of focus.
Furthermore, it is the wheel of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-cakra*), because all that is spoken through language is empty and cannot be expressed."
Thus, regarding the Wheel of Dharma spoken by the Blessed One, all these are the meanings of the Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, as for how many times and in what manner the Blessed One turned the Wheel of Dharma, that meaning shall now be explained.
The Wheel of Dharma has three turnings and twelve aspects.

"This is the Noble Truth of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering; this is the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering"—this is the first turning.

"This noble truth of suffering should be known; this origin of suffering should be abandoned; this cessation of suffering should be realized; this path leading to the cessation of suffering should be cultivated"—this is the second turning.

"This noble truth of suffering has been known; this origin of suffering has been abandoned; this cessation of suffering has been realized; this path leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated"—this is the third turning.
This explains the three turnings.
Likewise, there is knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path.

Thus, there is knowledge of the three turnings regarding the truth of suffering; likewise for the truth of origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path—there is knowledge of the three turnings for each. These are said to consist of twelve aspects.

Why is this? Because there are three turnings of knowledge regarding the Truth of Suffering through distinct modes of practice; likewise, there are three turnings of knowledge for the Truth of Origination, the Truth of Cessation, and the Truth of the Path through their respective distinct modes of practice. Thus, as explained, there are twelve aspects.
That which is called suffering refers to the five aggregates; the characteristic of suffering within these five aggregates is what is termed "suffering.
That characteristic of suffering is empty; to penetrate this emptiness is called the Noble Truth of the Knowledge of Suffering.
Those five aggregates, having craving as their cause and latent tendencies and views as their cause, are called "origination.

If one does not differentiate them, does not differentiate them, does not grasp them, and does not contact them—neither the cause of craving nor the cause of views—this is called the Noble Truth of the Knowledge of Origination.
If those five aggregates are ultimately exhausted and extinguished—neither coming from the past, nor going to the future, nor being apprehended in the present—this is called cessation.
To know them thus is called the Noble Truth of the Knowledge of Cessation.

Once this has been realized, one relies upon the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of its origin, and the knowledge of its cessation; that mark of equanimity and that non-dual knowledge is called the Noble Truth of the Knowledge of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
Furthermore, for what reason are those Noble Truths taught as neither few nor many?
To analyze them in such a manner would lead to an infinite regress.

Moreover, it is by knowing the Four Noble Truths in this way that one attains liberation; namely, by knowing suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and subsequently attaining the means [to that cessation].
These Four Noble Truths are explained in this manner according to their sequence.
Furthermore, what is their characteristic of equality?
They are called the Noble Truths because they are non-false dharmas; it is precisely because they are non-false that they are termed "truths" (*satya*).
Each and every self-characteristic is non-false; such non-false dharmas are the mark of equality.
Furthermore, there is the supreme mark. What is this supreme mark?
Suffering has the characteristic of oppression; origination has the characteristic of production; cessation has the characteristic of tranquility; and the path has the characteristic of emergence.
Furthermore, whether in direct or reverse order, the twelve links of dependent origination revolve accordingly.

Furthermore, the *Vaipulya-sūtra* states that correct discernment and the capacity for discernment, when not properly observed, give rise to ignorance; it is not that phenomena are produced [from nothing], and so on, up to the accumulation of the great mass of suffering.
With that existence and its cessation, the Dharma-wheel thus turns in twelve aspects.
If one knows this, the Three Jewels are complete.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One speaks of "turning" herein; why then does the Tathāgata, in the Dharma-gate of non-arising, state that all dharmas do not turn and do not revolve? One should know it thus: they ultimately do not arise.
In this sequential order, that meaning is now explained:
that is the teaching of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while this is the teaching of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Furthermore, it is the teaching for this specific occasion.
Furthermore, this was spoken for the purpose of treating those who have faith and acceptance;
since this meaning has already been explained, it is now being restated.
Moreover, this was spoken thus for the sake of bodhisattvas who are beginners, whereas those who have attained the great stages do not engage in such disputes.
If sentient beings and phenomena are all unattainable, then in what does the World-Honored One abide and maintain himself to turn the wheel of Dharma?
This meaning is now explained:

by means of great compassion, the Buddha neither grasps at sentient beings nor grasps at phenomena, yet he constantly abides in the maintenance of both sentient beings and phenomena while turning the wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, in the *Nāgarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the Blessed One stated: "The turning of the wheel of Dharma is like the turning of space.
Moreover, this is the Blessed One’s skillful means: he teaches that all phenomena, which are nameless, by means of names.
Therefore, the verse says:
"All phenomena are nameless; yet names are established to designate phenomena.
The World-Honored One does not grasp at sentient beings as a matter of natural law, yet he disciplines sentient beings and teaches the Dharma for their sake.
Although one does not grasp at phenomena, one constantly and extensively expounds all dharmas.

Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Vimalanāman Sūtra* state: "In order to know ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is taught; thus, there is no fault."

Furthermore, for what reason did the World-Honored One abandon that vast place adorned with various kinds of exquisite flower trees and filled with a great multitude of superior people, instead turning the Wheel of Dharma at the Deer Park beneath the shade of the Pāṭalī tree in Vārāṇasī, a place where few people dwell?
The meaning of this is now explained:

In the past, the World-Honored One already practiced extensive acts of giving at that place during sixty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* assemblies; furthermore, he had already made offerings there to sixty thousand *koṭi-nayuta* Buddhas; moreover, ninety-one billion *koṭi* Buddhas had turned the wheel of Dharma at that place, which was always abounding with tranquil sages.
Because there are such great merits as these, the World-Honored One turned the wheel of Dharma in that place.
This meaning has already been explained, yet it shall now be stated once more.
Furthermore, a verse in the *Vaipulya-sūtra* says:
“I have given alms at sixty thousand billion, nayutas of assemblies,
making offerings to sixty thousand billion, nayutas of Buddhas.”
Varanasi is a supreme place, where the most excellent ancient seers dwell;
it is a site for preaching the Dharma that devas, nāgas, and others of the highest rank constantly praise.
Ninety-one koṭis of eons ago, I recall the Unsurpassed Victor.
In this wondrous grove, he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Here dwell nayutas of tranquil and supreme sages who constantly reside within the Deer Park; therefore, it is named the Abode of Sages.
"In this supreme grove, he turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Having thus turned it, he did so for the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of people.
Furthermore, where did the Blessed One first sit when he turned the wheel of Dharma?
The meaning of this is now explained:
the Blessed One sat upon that great circular pavilion, on a lion throne adorned with immeasurable, pure, and wondrously colored precious gems, and there he turned the wheel of Dharma.
Where is this taught? It is stated thus in the *Vipula-saṃnipāta-sūtra*: "O bhikṣus!

There were earth-dwelling devas who, knowing that the Wheel of Dharma was about to be turned in Vārāṇasī for the sake of great benefit, prepared a great circular palace, adorned in various ways, vast and magnificent. That palace was seven hundred yojanas in length and breadth."
The devas of the void adorned [the space] with canopies, banners, and streamers.
In the sky above, eighty-four thousand celestial sons of the desire realm offered lion thrones to the Tathāgata.
Having made offerings to the Tathāgata, each one requested, saying:
"I pray that the Tathāgata will sit upon this seat of mine and turn the wheel of Dharma!
Each of the sons of heaven saw the World-Honored One sitting upon the lion throne they had offered and turning the wheel of Dharma.
“World-Honored One, you have thus fulfilled the intentions of all these sons of the gods.
Furthermore, when the World-Honored One turned the wheel of Dharma, how many sentient beings abandoned evil and practiced good?
The meaning of this shall now be explained.
There were five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya; furthermore, there were sixty billion devas, eighty billion devas from the realm of form (rūpadhātu), and eighty-four thousand billion human beings.
Where is this taught?
In that *Vipula-sūtra*, there is a verse which says:
“Ajñāta-kauṇḍinya and the others— these five bhikṣus.”
Six billion devas all attained the purity of the Dharma-eye;
Eight billion gods of the form realm attained the unsurpassed purity of the Dharma-eye;
Those people who attained the pure and supreme Dharma-eye numbered eighty-four billion.
To state it briefly: the sustaining of sentient beings is the manifestation of teaching sentient beings, while the sustaining of the Dharma is the manifestation of preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
the sustaining of sentient beings manifests the eighty-four thousand mental activities of sentient beings so that they may be known.
Regarding the "upholding of the Dharma": it is manifested to show that the light of the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma brings great benefit.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
the "upholding by sentient beings" is manifested to demonstrate the equality of all sentient beings.
The "Dharmasthititva" (Abiding of the Dharma) demonstrates the equality of all phenomena.
Furthermore, these two are manifested according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
*Dharmacakrapravartana-sūtra-upadeśa*, one fascicle.
